questions.q: How does sharding differ from Lesson 9's partitioning?
options: Sharding spreads data across genuinely separate storage instances; partitioning splits a table into chunks within one storage system
Sharding and partitioning are exactly the same technique with different names
Sharding only applies to dimension tables, never fact tables
Partitioning requires multiple servers, while sharding uses only one
questions.explain: Partitioning is folders inside one Delta table on one system; sharding is separate database servers, each holding only a slice.

questions.q: What makes a shard key a good choice?
options: It spreads both storage and traffic roughly evenly across all shards
It should always be a sequential, time-based column
It must be the same as the fact table's grain from Lesson 8
Any column works equally well as a shard key
questions.explain: A bad shard key concentrates storage and traffic onto one shard, defeating the entire point of sharding.

questions.q: What is a hot shard, specifically?
options: One shard absorbing a disproportionate share of traffic while the rest of the cluster sits nearly idle
A shard that has been permanently deleted
A shard optimized for OLAP rather than OLTP workloads
The first shard created when a database is initially set up
questions.explain: A sequential shard key like signup_date routes all new writes to the same shard, creating exactly this imbalance.

questions.q: Why does a hashed customer_id usually beat signup_date as a shard key?
options: A hash spreads customers evenly across shards, while signup_date sends every new write to the same 'today' shard
signup_date is not a valid data type for a shard key
customer_id can never be used as a shard key
Hashing always eliminates the need for sharding entirely
questions.explain: This is the hot shard problem in practice — a naturally clustered-in-time key concentrates load on one shard.

questions.q: When is sharding actually needed, rather than partitioning alone?
options: When no single server can hold the data or absorb the write volume, no matter how it's partitioned internally
Sharding should always be used by default, regardless of scale
Only when the data has no date column to partition by
Sharding is never needed if OLAP storage is used instead of OLTP
questions.explain: Sharding adds real operational cost — cross-shard joins and rebalancing — so it's worth it only once one well-partitioned server genuinely runs out of room.
